csharp-1.pitch: CLR runs the code, CTS defines the types, CLS keeps languages compatible.
csharp-1.definition: These are the three pillars of .NET's common runtime. The CLR (Common Language Runtime) is the virtual machine that executes managed code, handling JIT compilation, garbage collection and security. The CTS (Common Type System) defines how types are declared and used so all .NET languages share one type model. The CLS (Common Language Specification) is a subset of rules every language must follow so components written in C#, F# or VB can interoperate.
keyPoints: CLR: executes code, JIT + GC + security
CTS: common type rules across languages
Together they enable one runtime, many languages

csharp-7.pitch: Value types hold the data; reference types hold a pointer to it.
csharp-7.definition: Value types (int, struct, enum, bool) store their data directly and live on the stack or inline, so copying them copies the whole value. Reference types (class, string, array, delegate) store a reference to an object on the managed heap, so copying copies only the pointer and both variables share the same object. This difference drives how assignment, equality and method arguments behave.

csharp-8.pitch: Class = reference, Struct = value, Record = value-equality data type.
csharp-8.definition: A class is a reference type for objects with identity and behaviour, allocated on the heap. A struct is a value type for small, immutable, short-lived data, copied by value and usually stack-allocated. A record (C# 9+) is a reference type (or record struct) built for immutable data, giving value-based equality, with-expressions and concise syntax. You pick based on size, mutability and whether you want reference or value semantics.
keyPoints: Struct: value type, small immutable data
Use struct for tiny data, record for DTOs

csharp-9.pitch: Boxing wraps a value type in an object on the heap; unboxing unwraps it.
csharp-9.definition: Boxing is the implicit conversion of a value type (like int) into an object reference, which allocates a box on the managed heap and copies the value into it. Unboxing is the reverse cast back to the value type. They are expensive because each boxing causes a heap allocation and later GC pressure, plus the copy cost, so hot paths that box in loops (e.g. via non-generic collections or object) can hurt performance.

csharp-10.pitch: The GC automatically reclaims heap memory you no longer reference.
csharp-10.definition: The .NET garbage collector automatically frees managed heap memory that is no longer reachable, so you rarely free memory by hand. It is generational: Gen 0 holds new short-lived objects and is collected often and cheaply, survivors are promoted to Gen 1 then Gen 2 (long-lived), and large objects (>= 85KB) go on the Large Object Heap which is collected with Gen 2. A 'memory leak' in .NET usually means objects stay reachable (e.g. static references, undisposed event handlers) so the GC never collects them.
keyPoints: Gen 1: buffer between short and long lived
bestPractices: Unsubscribe events / dispose to avoid leaks
Avoid long-lived static references to large graphs
Reduce hot-path allocations to cut Gen 0 churn

csharp-11.pitch: Strings are immutable; use StringBuilder for heavy concatenation.
csharp-11.definition: A string in C# is immutable - every operation that 'changes' it actually creates a new string, which makes strings thread-safe and safe to share but means repeated concatenation allocates many objects. String interning stores one shared copy of identical literals in an intern pool so equal literals reference the same instance. For building strings in loops you use StringBuilder, which edits an internal buffer in place instead of allocating a new string each time.

code.note: StringBuilder mutates a buffer; string += in a loop would allocate 1000 strings.

keyPoints: Immutable: edits create a new string
Interning: shared copy of equal literals

csharp-15.pitch: OOP rests on encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.
csharp-15.definition: The four pillars of object-oriented programming organise code around objects. Encapsulation hides internal state behind a public interface; abstraction exposes only the essential behaviour and hides the details; inheritance lets a type reuse and extend another; and polymorphism lets one interface behave differently across types (via overriding or interfaces). Together they make code modular, reusable and easy to extend.
keyPoints: Inheritance: reuse and extend a base type

csharp-18.pitch: Interface = a contract; abstract class = a shared base with state.
csharp-18.definition: An interface defines a contract of members a type must implement, with no state and (historically) no implementation, and a class can implement many interfaces. An abstract class is a partially implemented base that can hold fields, constructors and shared logic, but a class can inherit only one. You choose an interface for capability and multiple inheritance, and an abstract class when you want to share state or default behaviour across related types.

csharp-25.pitch: Generics let you write type-safe code that works for any type.
csharp-25.definition: Generics let you parameterize classes and methods by type, so one implementation works for many types without boxing or casting. They give compile-time type safety and better performance than using object, and constraints (where T : ...) restrict what T can be so you can call its members. List<T>, Dictionary<TKey,TValue> and Func<T> are all generic.

code.snippet:
public T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>  // constraint enables CompareTo
    => a.CompareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;

int m = Max(3, 9);          // works for int...
string s = Max("a", "b");   // ...and string, type-safe
code.note: The where T : IComparable<T> constraint lets you call CompareTo on T.

csharp-26.pitch: LINQ queries are lazy until you actually enumerate them.
csharp-26.definition: LINQ uses deferred execution: building a query (Where, Select, etc.) does not run it - it only runs when you enumerate the result, e.g. in a foreach or via ToList/ToArray/Count/First. Immediate execution happens with those materializing operators that force evaluation right away. The pitfall is that a deferred query re-runs every time you enumerate it and reflects the latest source data, so capturing variables or expecting a snapshot can surprise you.

code.note: The query runs at ToList(), so it includes items added after it was defined.

keyPoints: Deferred queries re-run on each enumeration

csharp-28.pitch: IQueryable builds a DB query; IEnumerable filters in memory.
csharp-28.definition: IEnumerable<T> executes LINQ in memory using delegates, so with Entity Framework it would pull rows into the app and then filter. IQueryable<T> builds an expression tree that the provider (EF) translates into SQL, so filtering, sorting and paging run in the database and only the needed rows come back. That is why IQueryable is preferred in EF - it avoids loading whole tables into memory.

csharp-30.pitch: A delegate is a type-safe function pointer; an event wraps it safely.
csharp-30.definition: A delegate is a type that references one or more methods with a matching signature, so you can pass methods around and invoke them. An event is a restricted wrapper over a delegate that exposes only subscribe (+=) and unsubscribe (-=) to the outside, so subscribers cannot invoke it or overwrite other subscribers. In short, events use delegates under the hood but enforce the publisher/subscriber pattern safely.

csharp-31.pitch: Lambdas are inline functions; closures capture their surrounding variables.
csharp-31.definition: A lambda expression is a concise inline function (x => x * 2) you pass as a delegate. A closure is what happens when a lambda captures a variable from its enclosing scope - it captures the variable, not its value, which is the classic loop gotcha. Func, Action and Predicate are the built-in delegate types: Func<...,TResult> returns a value, Action<...> returns void, and Predicate<T> returns a bool.

code.snippet:
Func<int,int> square = x => x * x;     // returns a value
Action<string> log = s => Console.WriteLine(s); // returns void
Predicate<int> isEven = n => n % 2 == 0;        // returns bool
code.note: Func returns a result, Action returns void, Predicate returns a bool.

keyPoints: Closure: captures the variable, not its value

csharp-33.pitch: Use throw to preserve the stack trace; throw ex erases it.
csharp-33.definition: C# exception handling uses try/catch/finally to detect, handle and clean up after errors, with finally always running for resource cleanup. Inside a catch, 'throw;' rethrows the current exception and preserves the original stack trace, while 'throw ex;' resets the stack trace to the rethrow point, hiding where the error really started. Best practice is to catch only what you can handle and rethrow with 'throw;' (or wrap in a new exception with the original as InnerException).

code.note: 'throw;' preserves where the error originated; 'throw ex;' loses it.

keyPoints: Catch only what you can handle

csharp-34.pitch: IDisposable + using free unmanaged resources deterministically.
csharp-34.definition: IDisposable defines a Dispose() method for releasing unmanaged resources (files, sockets, DB connections) deterministically, and a using statement calls Dispose automatically at the end of the block even on exceptions. Finalize (the destructor) is a safety net the GC calls non-deterministically if Dispose was missed, but it delays collection and should be avoided unless you hold unmanaged handles. The standard pattern is to implement IDisposable and rely on using rather than finalizers.

code.note: using guarantees Dispose() runs at the end of the block, even on errors.

csharp-35.pitch: await frees the thread while an operation runs, then resumes after it.
csharp-35.definition: async/await is C#'s model for non-blocking asynchronous code. The compiler rewrites an async method into a state machine: when you await an incomplete Task, the method returns to its caller and the current thread is released instead of blocking, and when the awaited operation completes a continuation resumes the method where it left off. This lets a server handle many concurrent requests with few threads, which is why I/O-bound work should be async.
steps: Compiler turns the method into a state machine
await checks if the Task is already complete
If not, the method returns; the thread is freed
When the Task completes, a continuation is scheduled
Execution resumes after the await with the result

code.note: At each await the thread is released; the method resumes when the I/O completes.

csharp-36.pitch: Tasks are high-level async work; Threads are raw OS threads.
csharp-36.definition: A Thread is a dedicated OS thread you create and manage directly - powerful but heavy. The ThreadPool is a managed pool of reusable worker threads that avoids the cost of creating threads per work item. A Task is a high-level abstraction representing async work that usually runs on the ThreadPool and composes with async/await. ValueTask is a lighter-weight alternative to Task for hot paths that often complete synchronously, avoiding an allocation.
keyPoints: Thread: raw OS thread, heavy, manual
ValueTask: low-alloc Task for hot paths

csharp-39.pitch: Pick the lightest sync primitive that covers your sharing scenario.
csharp-39.definition: These are .NET's thread-synchronization primitives, from lightest to heaviest. lock is syntactic sugar over Monitor for mutual exclusion within a process; Interlocked does atomic operations (increment, exchange) without a lock; Mutex is a heavier, OS-level lock that can work across processes; Semaphore/SemaphoreSlim limit how many threads enter a region at once; and ReaderWriterLockSlim allows many readers but one writer. You choose the lightest one that fits to minimize contention.

csharp-2.pitch: C# code goes source -> IL -> JIT -> native, run by the CLR.
csharp-2.definition: A C# program is compiled in two stages. First the C# compiler (Roslyn) turns source code into platform-neutral Intermediate Language (IL) plus metadata, packaged in an assembly (.dll/.exe). At runtime the CLR loads the assembly and the JIT compiler converts IL into native machine code on demand, which the CPU then executes while the GC manages memory. This two-step model is what makes .NET cross-platform and language-agnostic.

diagram.title: Compilation to execution
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[C# Source] --> B[Roslyn Compiler]
  B --> C[IL + Metadata]
  C --> D[CLR + JIT]
  D --> E[Native Code]
  E --> F[CPU Execution]

steps: C# compiler turns source into IL + metadata
IL is packaged into an assembly (.dll/.exe)
CLR loads the assembly at runtime
JIT compiles IL to native code on demand
CPU executes native code; GC manages memory

csharp-3.pitch: The JIT compiles IL to native code at runtime, method by method.
csharp-3.definition: The Just-In-Time compiler turns IL into native machine code at runtime, typically the first time each method is called, then caches it so later calls reuse the native version. Variants include normal JIT (compile on first use), pre-JIT/AOT (compile everything ahead of time, e.g. ReadyToRun or Native AOT), and tiered compilation, where .NET first emits quick code then re-JITs hot methods with deeper optimizations. This balances startup time against peak performance.
keyPoints: Normal JIT: compile each method on first call
Pre-JIT / AOT: compile ahead (ReadyToRun, Native AOT)
Tiered: quick code first, optimize hot paths later
Native code is cached and reused

csharp-4.pitch: Managed code runs under the CLR; unmanaged code runs directly on the OS.
csharp-4.definition: Managed code is compiled to IL and executed by the CLR, which provides garbage collection, type safety and security. Unmanaged code (C/C++, COM, OS APIs) compiles straight to native machine code and manages its own memory, running outside the CLR's control. C# is managed, but it can call unmanaged code via P/Invoke or interop when it needs native libraries.

csharp-5.pitch: Modern C# (8-13) adds null safety, records, pattern matching and more.
csharp-5.definition: Recent C# versions focus on safety, conciseness and performance. Highlights: C# 8 added nullable reference types, switch expressions and default interface methods; C# 9 brought records, init-only setters and top-level statements; C# 10-11 added global usings, file-scoped namespaces, required members and raw string literals; C# 12-13 added primary constructors, collection expressions and further refinements. Together they cut boilerplate and make null handling explicit.
keyPoints: C# 10-11: global usings, required members, raw strings

csharp-6.pitch: var is compile-time inferred, dynamic is runtime, explicit is fixed.
csharp-6.definition: All three declare variables but differ in when the type is resolved. var is still statically typed - the compiler infers the type at compile time from the right-hand side, so it is fully type-checked. Explicit typing states the type directly. dynamic bypasses compile-time checking entirely and resolves members at runtime, which is flexible for interop/COM but loses IntelliSense and can throw at runtime.
keyPoints: dynamic: resolved at runtime, no compile check
dynamic suits interop/COM, risks runtime errors

csharp-12.pitch: const is compile-time, readonly is run-time, static readonly is shared.
csharp-12.definition: All three create values you cannot reassign, but they differ in when the value is set. const is a compile-time constant baked into callers, so it must be a literal and never changes. readonly is set once at runtime (in the declaration or constructor), so it can use computed or injected values per instance. static readonly is a single readonly value shared across all instances, set in a static constructor.

csharp-13.pitch: Access modifiers control where a member can be seen and used.
csharp-13.definition: C# access modifiers set the visibility of types and members. public is visible everywhere; private is only inside the same type; protected is the type plus derived types; internal is the same assembly; protected internal is protected OR internal (derived types or same assembly); and private protected is protected AND internal (derived types within the same assembly). Defaulting to the most restrictive level that still works is good encapsulation.
keyPoints: protected internal: derived OR same assembly
private protected: derived AND same assembly

csharp-14.pitch: ref passes by reference, out returns a value, in passes read-only.
csharp-14.definition: These modifiers change how arguments are passed. ref passes a variable by reference so the method can read and modify it, and it must be initialized before the call. out also passes by reference but the method must assign it before returning, so it is used to return extra values. in passes by reference as read-only, avoiding a copy of large structs while preventing modification.

csharp-16.pitch: Overloading is compile-time, overriding is run-time, hiding shadows.
csharp-16.definition: These three look similar but resolve differently. Overloading means several methods with the same name but different parameters, resolved at compile time. Overriding replaces a virtual/abstract base method in a derived class (override keyword) and is resolved at runtime via polymorphism. Method hiding uses the new keyword to shadow a base member without polymorphism, so the version called depends on the reference's compile-time type.
keyPoints: Hiding (new): shadow base member, not polymorphic

csharp-17.pitch: Constructor chaining reuses one constructor from another.
csharp-17.definition: Constructor chaining is calling one constructor from another to avoid duplicating initialization - this(...) calls another constructor in the same class, and base(...) calls a base-class constructor. In an inheritance hierarchy, construction runs base-first: the base constructor executes before the derived one, so the object is built from the most-base type up. Field initializers run before the constructor body.
steps: Derived constructor is invoked
It calls base(...) (implicitly if omitted)
Base field initializers + base constructor run first
Then derived field initializers
Finally the derived constructor body

csharp-19.pitch: Explicit implementation hides an interface member behind the interface.
csharp-19.definition: Explicit interface implementation implements a member as InterfaceName.Member, so it is only accessible when the object is referenced through that interface, not through the class. You use it to resolve name clashes when a type implements two interfaces with the same member, or to keep an interface member out of the class's public surface. It cannot have an access modifier.
csharp-19.when: When two interfaces share a member name, or to hide an interface member from the class's public API.

csharp-20.pitch: The diamond problem is ambiguous multiple inheritance; C# avoids it.
csharp-20.definition: The diamond problem occurs when a type inherits the same member from two paths, leaving it ambiguous which to use. C# sidesteps it by not allowing multiple class inheritance - a class has one base. A type can implement many interfaces, and if two interfaces declare the same default method, C# requires you to resolve it explicitly, so ambiguity is a compile error you must fix.
keyPoints: Problem: same member inherited via two paths
C# allows only single class inheritance
Clashing default methods must be resolved explicitly

csharp-21.pitch: static members belong to the type, not to any instance.
csharp-21.definition: The static keyword ties members to the type itself rather than to instances. A static field is one shared value across all instances; a static method is called on the type and cannot touch instance data; a static constructor runs once to initialize static state before first use; and a static class cannot be instantiated and holds only static members (e.g. utility/helper classes like Math).
keyPoints: Static field: one shared value for all instances
Static method: called on the type, no instance data
Static constructor: runs once before first use
Static class: no instances, only static members

csharp-22.pitch: Properties wrap fields with logic; init-only allows set only at creation.
csharp-22.definition: These are ways to expose data on a type. A field is a raw variable; a property wraps get/set accessors around backing data so you can add validation or logic. An auto-implemented property (public int X { get; set; }) lets the compiler generate the backing field. An init-only property (get; init;) can be set only during object initialization, enabling immutable objects you still construct with object initializers.

csharp-23.pitch: Pick the collection by access pattern: index, key, order or uniqueness.
csharp-23.definition: Each collection optimizes a different access pattern. Arrays are fixed-size, contiguous, fast index access. List<T> is a resizable array with fast index access and amortized append. LinkedList<T> gives O(1) insert/remove at known nodes but slow indexing. Dictionary<TKey,TValue> and the legacy non-generic HashTable give O(1) key lookups via hashing. HashSet<T> stores unique items with O(1) membership tests.
keyPoints: Array: fixed size, fast index access
LinkedList<T>: O(1) node insert/remove, slow index

csharp-24.pitch: These interfaces add capability as you go from read-only to queryable.
csharp-24.definition: These collection interfaces form a capability ladder. IEnumerable<T> only supports forward iteration. ICollection<T> adds Count, Add and Remove. IList<T> adds index access and insertion. IReadOnlyCollection<T> exposes Count without mutation. IQueryable<T> represents a query that a provider (like EF) translates to another language such as SQL. You expose the least capable interface that the caller needs.
csharp-24.when: Return the least capable interface a caller needs; IQueryable only for remote/DB queries.

csharp-27.pitch: These LINQ operators filter, project and pick elements differently.
csharp-27.definition: These are common LINQ operators. Where filters by a predicate. Select projects each item; SelectMany projects and flattens nested sequences into one. Any returns whether any item matches; Count returns how many. First/FirstOrDefault return the first match (FirstOrDefault gives a default instead of throwing when empty). Single/SingleOrDefault expect exactly one match and throw if there are more than one.

csharp-29.pitch: A delegate references methods; multicast holds several; events wrap it.
csharp-29.definition: A delegate is a type-safe reference to one or more methods with a matching signature. A multicast delegate chains multiple methods with += and invokes them all in order on a single call (for non-void delegates only the last return value is kept). An event is a restricted delegate that exposes only subscribe/unsubscribe to outside code, enforcing the publisher/subscriber pattern safely.

csharp-32.pitch: Extension methods add methods to a type without modifying it.
csharp-32.definition: An extension method lets you call a static method as if it were an instance method on an existing type, using the this modifier on the first parameter, without changing or inheriting that type. LINQ is the classic example - Where and Select are extension methods on IEnumerable<T>. They are great for fluent helpers (string utilities, builders) but should not hide important behaviour.

code.note: The this modifier on the first parameter turns a static method into an extension.

keyPoints: Add methods without changing the type
First param uses the this modifier
Must live in a static class

csharp-37.pitch: These are the everyday tools for controlling and combining async work.
csharp-37.definition: These help you control async flow. ConfigureAwait(false) tells await not to resume on the original synchronization context, which avoids deadlocks and overhead in library code. A CancellationToken lets callers cooperatively cancel long-running work. Task.WhenAll runs tasks in parallel and completes when all finish (great for fan-out); Task.WhenAny completes when the first finishes (useful for timeouts or first-response-wins).

code.snippet:
var results = await Task.WhenAll(ids.Select(GetAsync)); // run all in parallel

await DoWorkAsync(token);          // honors cancellation
await call.ConfigureAwait(false);  // don't capture the context

csharp-38.pitch: Concurrency needs synchronization to stay correct and deadlock-free.
csharp-38.definition: These are the core concurrency concepts. Multithreading runs multiple threads at once to use CPU cores or overlap I/O. A race condition is when the outcome depends on unsynchronized timing of threads touching shared state. A deadlock is when threads wait on each other's locks forever. Thread synchronization (locks, semaphores, atomics) coordinates access to shared data so results stay correct.
keyPoints: Deadlock: threads wait on each other forever
bestPractices: Lock the smallest scope for the shortest time
Always acquire multiple locks in the same order
Prefer immutable data / concurrent collections

csharp-40.pitch: Reflection inspects and invokes types at runtime; DI relies on it.
csharp-40.definition: Reflection lets code examine assemblies, types and members at runtime and create instances or invoke methods dynamically. DI containers use it to discover a type's constructor parameters and instantiate the right dependencies automatically. It is powerful for frameworks, serializers and DI, but it is slower than direct calls and bypasses compile-time checks, so it should be used sparingly (and cached) in hot paths.
csharp-40.how: A DI container reads a type's constructor via reflection, resolves each parameter type from its registrations, then uses Activator/compiled expressions to create the instance.
keyPoints: Create instances and invoke methods dynamically
Slower than direct calls - cache it

csharp-41.pitch: Assemblies are .NET's deployment unit; strong names/GAC enable sharing.
csharp-41.definition: An assembly (.dll/.exe) is the unit of deployment and versioning in .NET, containing IL, metadata and a manifest. Strong naming signs an assembly with a key pair to give it a unique identity and tamper-check. The GAC (Global Assembly Cache) is a machine-wide store for shared strong-named assemblies on .NET Framework. The CLR loads assemblies on demand by probing configured paths or the GAC.
keyPoints: CLR loads assemblies lazily on demand

csharp-42.pitch: Stream APIs read/write data in chunks; never load a 10GB file at once.
csharp-42.definition: FileStream reads and writes raw bytes to a file; StreamReader and StreamWriter wrap a stream to read and write text with encoding. To process a huge file you stream it - read line by line or in buffered chunks so memory stays flat regardless of file size, ideally with async I/O. Reading the whole file into memory (File.ReadAllText) would blow up on a 10GB file.
bestPractices: Stream with ReadLineAsync or buffered reads
Keep memory flat - don't buffer the whole file
Use async I/O and dispose streams with using

csharp-43.pitch: These are modern C# features for performance and expressive code.
csharp-43.definition: These modern features improve performance and readability. Span<T> and Memory<T> give safe, allocation-free views over contiguous memory (arrays, stack, strings), avoiding copies. A ref struct (like Span<T>) is stack-only so it cannot be boxed or captured. Pattern matching and switch expressions let you branch concisely on type, shape and values, replacing long if/else chains.

csharp-44.pitch: Dictionary/HashSet use hashing with buckets to get O(1) lookups.
csharp-44.definition: Dictionary<TKey,TValue> and HashSet<T> store items in buckets indexed by the key's hash code, giving average O(1) insert and lookup. The hash maps a key to a bucket; within a bucket, items are kept in a chain and compared with Equals to find the exact match. Collisions (different keys, same bucket) are resolved by chaining, and the structure resizes/rehashes when it gets too full to keep chains short.
csharp-44.how: Compute key.GetHashCode() -> map to a bucket -> within the bucket, walk the chain comparing with Equals -> resize and rehash when the load factor grows.
keyPoints: Items placed in buckets by hash code

csharp-45.pitch: Cut allocations and reuse buffers to reduce GC pressure.
csharp-45.definition: GC pressure comes from allocating many short-lived objects, which forces frequent Gen 0 collections. You reduce it by allocating less and reusing more: prefer structs/Span<T> for transient data, pool reusable objects (ArrayPool, object pools), avoid boxing and unnecessary LINQ allocations in hot paths, use StringBuilder for string building, and stream large data instead of buffering it. Always profile first to target the real hotspots.
keyPoints: Allocate less in hot paths (Span<T>, structs)
Avoid boxing and LINQ churn in loops
Stream large data, don't buffer it
bestPractices: Profile allocations before optimizing
Reuse buffers instead of re-allocating
Avoid async-over-sync and needless captures

csharp-46.pitch: Find what stays reachable, then break the reference holding it.
csharp-46.definition: A .NET memory leak means objects remain reachable so the GC never frees them - common causes are static collections that keep growing, event handlers never unsubscribed, and undisposed resources. To fix it you reproduce the growth, capture memory snapshots over time (dotnet-gcdump, dotMemory, PerfView), compare snapshots to find the type that keeps growing, trace its GC roots to the offending reference, then remove it (unsubscribe, dispose, or scope the cache).
steps: Reproduce and confirm memory grows over time
Take heap snapshots (dotnet-gcdump / dotMemory)
Diff snapshots to find the growing type
Trace its GC roots to the holding reference
Fix it: unsubscribe, dispose, or bound the cache
bestPractices: Unsubscribe events and dispose resources
Bound caches with size/expiry
Watch static collections that only grow

csharp-47.pitch: Reproduce, capture thread stacks, find the lock cycle, then order locks.
csharp-47.definition: An intermittent deadlock is two or more threads each holding a lock the other needs, so they wait forever. To resolve it you capture the process while it is hung (a dump or dotnet-dump), inspect the thread stacks to see which threads are blocked on which locks, identify the cyclic wait, then fix the root cause - usually by acquiring locks in a consistent global order, reducing lock scope, using timeouts (Monitor.TryEnter), or switching to lock-free/async patterns.
steps: Reproduce, then capture a dump while hung
Inspect thread stacks (dotnet-dump / WinDbg)
Find the threads blocked on each other's locks
Identify the cyclic lock-wait
Fix: consistent lock order, timeouts, smaller scope
bestPractices: Always acquire multiple locks in one global order
Use Monitor.TryEnter with a timeout
Avoid blocking on async (.Result/.Wait)

csharp-48.pitch: Use a concurrent store with expiry, sized to avoid unbounded growth.
csharp-48.definition: A thread-safe, high-performance in-memory cache stores values keyed for fast lookup while staying correct under concurrency and bounded in size. I would build on ConcurrentDictionary for lock-free reads and fine-grained writes, add per-entry expiry (absolute/sliding) and a size limit with an eviction policy (LRU), and use atomic GetOrAdd to avoid duplicate work on cache misses. MemoryCache already provides much of this out of the box.

code.snippet: var value = _cache.GetOrAdd(key, k => Load(k)); // atomic, computes once on miss

keyPoints: GetOrAdd to avoid duplicate work on misses
Size limit + LRU eviction to stay bounded

csharp-49.pitch: Stream rows in batches; never load millions of records into memory.
csharp-49.definition: To process millions of rows efficiently you avoid loading them all at once and keep memory flat by streaming. Read with a server-side / streaming query (no buffering), process in batches, and project only the columns you need. Use async enumeration (IAsyncEnumerable / DbDataReader), avoid change-tracking in EF (AsNoTracking), and write results in bulk. This keeps memory constant regardless of how many rows there are.
keyPoints: Stream rows, don't buffer the whole set
Process in batches with constant memory
bestPractices: Never ToList() millions of rows
Disable EF change tracking for read-only scans
Tune batch size to balance throughput vs memory

csharp-50.pitch: Stateless services, async I/O, smart caching, and hard-won lessons.
csharp-50.definition: A high-scale C# system I would describe is a set of stateless ASP.NET Core services behind a load balancer, communicating via a message queue for async work, with a distributed cache in front of the database and async I/O throughout. The concurrency model is async/await plus the ThreadPool so a few threads serve many requests; performance comes from caching, paging, AsNoTracking queries and reduced allocations. The hardest challenges are usually cache invalidation, avoiding hot partitions, and taming GC pauses under load.

  C[Clients] --> LB[Load Balancer]
  LB --> S1[Service]
  LB --> S2[Service]
  S1 --> Q[Message Queue]
  S1 --> Cache[(Distributed Cache)]
  S1 --> DB[(Database)]
  S2 --> Cache
  S2 --> DB

csharp-50.realWorld: On one system, moving hot reads to a distributed cache and making the data layer fully async cut database load by ~60% and let the same hardware handle 3x the traffic.
keyPoints: Stateless services behind a load balancer
Async I/O + ThreadPool for high concurrency
Distributed cache in front of the DB
Wins: caching, paging, AsNoTracking, fewer allocations
